To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) narrative self-evaluation of one's abilities (i.e., self-efficacy) is a distinct construct from narrative self-evaluation about one's behaviors and characteristics, (2) narrative self-efficacy is associated with less grief over time and, more specifically, (3) the ability to evaluate one's abilities positively appears to neutralize the impact of negative narrative evaluations of behaviors and characteristics on grief.

self-efficacy beliefs, which are self-evaluations that are about one's abilities (what one can do or be), are more strongly associated with positive psychological outcomes (less grief) than self-evaluations about one's behaviors (what one does) or one's characteristics (what one is).
self-efficacy, as a narrative construct, is associated with lower levels of grief over time and is a more potent buffer against the negative effects of grief than other self-evaluations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that self-efficacy plays in the narrative construction of identity.
the role of self-efficacious thinking in narrative identity construction during times of crisis and how this thinking relates to grief.
the role of narrative self-evaluation in psychological adaptation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-efficacy is a critical aspect of psychological adaptation to loss and is a distinct form of self-evaluation that may be more effective in the face of loss than other forms of self-evaluation.
this study provides evidence that the self-efficacy construct is distinct from other self-evaluations in the narrative domain.
the narrative differentiation of self-efficacies is associated with psychological health during times of bereavement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the narrative differentiation of self-efficacious abilities from other self-evaluations is associated with less grief and better adaptation to bereavement.
self-efficacy is an important factor in how people think about themselves and how they cope during times of crisis.
people who can do things, do things, and are good people, tend to be better off psychologically.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way we talk to ourselves about what we are able to do is an important part of how well we cope with major life changes.
self-efficacy is a powerful force in shaping the way people think and feel about themselves and their lives, and it has important implications for psychological health.
self-efficacy may be more than a psychological construct.
